statements.section: pgvector: PostgreSQL integration and approximate-search trade-offs
statements.statement: Keeping retrieval in PostgreSQL is attractive when an application already uses Postgres and wants vector search alongside its existing data; Supabase, for example, supports the pgvector extension as part of its Postgres offering [F-a992d87b]. pgvector performs exact nearest-neighbor search by default, with perfect recall, while approximate indexes trade some recall for speed [F-638ceefd, F-65d064f5].

statements.section: pgvector: PostgreSQL integration and approximate-search trade-offs
statements.statement: The approximate-index choice has a build-versus-query trade-off: HNSW offers a better speed–recall trade-off than IVFFlat but takes longer to build and uses more memory; IVFFlat builds faster and uses less memory but has a weaker speed–recall trade-off [F-f4106ba6, F-75bff3e5].
statements.reason: The source explicitly compares HNSW and IVFFlat on speed–recall performance, build time, and memory use.

statements.reason: The source identifies Pinecone’s storage and read/write units, Weaviate’s storage and vector-dimension charges, and Qdrant’s hourly charges for allocated resources.

statements.section: Pricing and deployment costs at a glance
statements.statement: The estimates below are planning figures rather than quotes, and bills can change with dimensions, replication and query rate [F-4217ce47, F-eda77937].
statements.reason: The sources call the figures planning estimates rather than quotes and say bills vary with dimensions, replication, and query rate.

statements.section: Pricing and deployment costs at a glance
statements.statement: **Pinecone.** Builder is a flat $20 per month, with no overages: it includes 10 serverless indexes, 10 GB of organization storage and 100 namespaces per index, and usage beyond its limits is blocked rather than billed [F-2388a4c0, F-87414f40, F-2c8d7426].
statements.reason: Pinecone’s documentation states the $20 flat fee, all three limits, and that excess usage is blocked rather than billed.

statements.section: Pricing and deployment costs at a glance
statements.statement: Standard has a $50 monthly minimum usage commitment and Enterprise a $500 minimum [F-78dbe22d, F-d5a57d20].
statements.reason: The documentation lists $50 and $500 monthly minimums for Standard and Enterprise, respectively.

statements.section: Pricing and deployment costs at a glance
statements.statement: Serverless charges for read units, write units, storage and egress; idle indexes incur no usage cost [F-d156fcec, F-1ec78925].
statements.reason: Pinecone lists read units, write units, storage, and egress as serverless usage metrics and says idle indexes cost nothing.

statements.section: Pricing and deployment costs at a glance
statements.statement: Standard’s optional HIPAA add-on costs $190 per month, while HIPAA compliance is included with Enterprise [F-625f4dc9].
statements.reason: The documentation states that the Standard HIPAA add-on costs $190 per month and HIPAA compliance is included with Enterprise.

statements.section: Pricing and deployment costs at a glance
statements.statement: If the estimate includes Pinecone Assistant, Starter’s monthly allowances are 500,000 chat input tokens, 300,000 chat output tokens, 500,000 context retrieval tokens and 1,000 ingestion units [F-7408af5f].
statements.reason: The cited Assistant passage lists exactly those monthly Starter allowances.

statements.section: Pricing and deployment costs at a glance
statements.statement: SpendArk estimates about $70 per month for a 10-million-vector serverless index with 768-dimensional embeddings, moderate queries and one replica, but notes that separately metered reads raise costs for query-heavy workloads [F-eda77937, F-ff8e0c51].
statements.reason: SpendArk gives the stated workload assumptions, the roughly $70 estimate, and the warning about separately metered reads.

statements.section: Pricing and deployment costs at a glance
statements.statement: By contrast, pecollective.com estimates $300–$800 per month or more for at least 10 million vectors and over 100,000 daily queries, with heavy writes or complex filtered queries potentially adding cost [F-298a41ca].
statements.reason: The source estimates $300–$800 per month for that scale, with potentially higher costs for heavy writes or complex filtered queries.

statements.section: Pricing and deployment costs at a glance
statements.statement: **Qdrant.** Its Cloud free tier provides 0.5 vCPU, 1 GB RAM and 4 GB disk [F-fe5290bf].
statements.reason: The source lists 0.5 vCPU, 1 GB RAM, and 4 GB disk for Qdrant Cloud’s free tier.

statements.section: Pricing and deployment costs at a glance
statements.statement: According to ranksquire.com, Cloud Standard bills hourly for provisioned resources rather than per query or write, with estimated monthly costs of $30–$60 for a 2 GB cluster and $120–$200 for an 8 GB cluster [F-5bdc36cc, F-cfd15ee3].
statements.reason: Ranksquire describes hourly resource-based Standard billing with no per-query or per-write charge and gives both monthly ranges.

statements.section: Pricing and deployment costs at a glance
statements.statement: Qdrant Hybrid Cloud is custom-priced and runs on customer infrastructure while Qdrant manages operations; self-hosted Qdrant OSS has no license fee but requires infrastructure spending [F-aa887cfc, F-83d60a27].
statements.reason: The source describes custom-priced Hybrid Cloud on customer infrastructure and free OSS licensing with compute infrastructure costs.

statements.section: Pricing and deployment costs at a glance
statements.statement: For sizing, ranksquire.com estimates that one million unquantized, 1,536-dimensional float32 vectors require roughly 8 GB RAM in production, including HNSW overhead [F-c3b8e99a].
statements.reason: Ranksquire estimates approximately 8 GB RAM including HNSW overhead for the specified unquantized production workload.

statements.section: Pricing and deployment costs at a glance
statements.statement: **Weaviate.** Its Cloud model, updated in October 2025, bills for stored vector dimensions, persistent object storage and backup storage [F-7a551894].
statements.reason: The source dates the pricing update to October 2025 and names vector dimensions, persistent object storage, and backup storage as billing components.

statements.section: Pricing and deployment costs at a glance
statements.statement: As of April 2026, ranksquire.com listed Flex at a $45 monthly minimum plus $0.01668 per million vector dimensions per month; Plus at a $280 monthly minimum with an annual commitment; and Premium at custom pricing [F-f30fc60a, F-289ff289].
statements.reason: The April 2026 source gives the stated Flex rate and minimum, Plus annual minimum, and Premium custom pricing.

statements.section: Pricing and deployment costs at a glance
statements.statement: In that source’s worked Flex example, five million 1,536-dimensional vectors with two replicas cost about $312 per month without Binary Quantization versus about $64 with it; it attributes the difference to approximately 97% lower dimension billing, while object and backup storage remain in the calculation [F-1f6aa1f7, F-b3cd54c9].
statements.reason: The worked example gives both totals, the roughly 97% dimension-cost reduction, and unchanged object and backup storage costs.

statements.section: Pricing and deployment costs at a glance
statements.statement: Ranksquire.com separately estimates $40–$120 per month for self-hosted Weaviate on DigitalOcean, depending on cluster size [F-5cd12dc0].
statements.reason: Ranksquire’s comparison lists self-hosted Weaviate on DigitalOcean at $40–$120 per month depending on cluster size.

statements.section: Pricing and deployment costs at a glance
statements.statement: **pgvector.** Its deployment estimate depends on the PostgreSQL host chosen: SpendArk’s comparable planning scenario puts pgvector on RDS at about $120 per month for 10 million vectors, using 768-dimensional embeddings, moderate queries and one replica without quantization [F-eda77937].
statements.reason: SpendArk’s RDS estimate is roughly $120 per month under the stated workload assumptions and without quantization; the host-dependence is a direct interpretation of that hosting-specific estimate.

statements.section: Pricing and deployment costs at a glance
statements.statement: As another hosting price point, Rivestack advertises fixed per-node pricing from $29 per month without usage metering [F-aff0111c].
statements.reason: The source describes Rivestack’s fixed per-node monthly pricing without usage metering, starting at $29.

statements.section: Pricing and deployment costs at a glance
statements.statement: These examples should not be treated as interchangeable bills: the estimate must hold vector dimensions, replication, query and write volume, storage and the chosen infrastructure constant where possible [F-eda77937, F-d156fcec, F-5bdc36cc, F-7a551894].
statements.reason: The sources show different billing bases and identify dimensions, replication, traffic, storage, and infrastructure as cost drivers, directly supporting the comparison guidance.

statements.section: Performance evidence: compare workloads, not headline QPS
statements.statement: Published throughput figures do not form a matched ranking of these databases: according to Tech Insider, it found no neutral benchmark of Pinecone, Weaviate, and Qdrant side by side under matched conditions as of August 2026 [F-056a0568].
statements.reason: Tech Insider says it found no neutral, matched, side-by-side benchmark of the three as of August 2026.

statements.section: Performance evidence: compare workloads, not headline QPS
statements.statement: The same source says ann-benchmarks.com does not maintain an always-current comparison of those three managed services and that Pinecone’s proprietary index cannot be tested outside its managed API [F-1dbc7214].
statements.reason: The source makes both claims about ann-benchmarks.com and Pinecone’s managed API.

statements.section: Performance evidence: compare workloads, not headline QPS
statements.statement: Recall targets, vector dimensions, corpus size, hardware, filters, concurrency, and the steps surrounding vector search therefore matter when interpreting a result [F-cfd832b8, F-f7d6fea2, F-53a373a8, F-267cb138].
statements.reason: The cited texts describe differing recall targets, dimensions, corpus sizes, hardware, filters and concurrency, as well as reranking latency.

statements.section: Performance evidence: compare workloads, not headline QPS
statements.statement: A 2026 comparison by kalviumlabs.ai reports approximately 850 QPS and 8 ms p95 for Qdrant versus 380 QPS and 18 ms p95 for Weaviate, citing Qdrant-published HNSW tests on one million 768-dimensional vectors at approximately 99% recall [F-e5ac8e4c].
statements.reason: The test conditions and figures match, but the supplied source text does not date the kalviumlabs.ai comparison to 2026.

statements.section: Performance evidence: compare workloads, not headline QPS
statements.statement: Its separate production measurements, on 500,000–one million 1,536-dimensional vectors, put pgvector HNSW at approximately 220 QPS and 48 ms p95, pgvector HNSW with four parallel workers at 360 QPS and 58 ms p95, pgvector IVFFlat at 90 QPS and 70 ms p95, and Pinecone Serverless in us-east-1 at 340 QPS and 28 ms p95 [F-36a8ef21].
statements.reason: The production-measurement table gives the stated corpus range, dimensions, configurations and figures.

statements.section: Performance evidence: compare workloads, not headline QPS
statements.statement: The page specifies a one-million-vector, 1,536-dimensional, cosine-distance default unless otherwise noted, but says the cited Qdrant tests used 768-dimensional vectors on Qdrant’s hardware; its pgvector and Pinecone figures came from production systems, whereas its Qdrant and Weaviate figures relied on Qdrant publications and spot checks [F-cfd832b8, F-fb1cbc36].
statements.reason: The page states the default conditions, the exception for Qdrant’s tests, and the different sources of its figures.

statements.section: Performance evidence: compare workloads, not headline QPS
statements.statement: These are different measurements, not a controlled four-way result [F-cfd832b8, F-fb1cbc36].
statements.reason: The source distinguishes Qdrant-published tests on its hardware from separate production measurements with different vector dimensions.

statements.section: Performance evidence: compare workloads, not headline QPS
statements.statement: A different 50-million-vector comparison at 99% recall cited Qdrant at 41 QPS and pgvectorscale—not pgvector alone—at 471 QPS [F-e06d5b0d].
statements.reason: Tech Insider gives the 50-million-vector, 99%-recall figures and identifies the other engine as pgvectorscale.

statements.section: Performance evidence: compare workloads, not headline QPS
statements.statement: According to checkthat.ai, the comparison used identical AWS hardware and measured 41.47 versus 471.57 QPS, respectively, while Qdrant’s tail latency was 39–48% lower [F-ecb84495].
statements.reason: checkthat.ai states the identical-AWS-hardware comparison, both precise QPS figures and the tail-latency difference.

statements.section: Performance evidence: compare workloads, not headline QPS
statements.statement: The contrast with the one-million-vector figures underscores why a recall-constrained, larger-corpus test should not be read as a universal throughput ranking [F-e06d5b0d, F-e5ac8e4c].
statements.reason: The sources describe materially different corpus sizes and test conditions, supporting the caution against a universal ranking.

statements.section: Performance evidence: compare workloads, not headline QPS
statements.statement: LambdaDB’s May 19, 2026 test provides another workload-specific view: according to LambdaDB, it queried a preloaded ten-million-vector English subset of Cohere Wikipedia 2023-11 embeddings at 1,024 dimensions, testing 1–32 concurrent clients for 30 seconds each; its separate upsert workload used one million vectors, 2,000-document batches, and 64 concurrent writers [F-f7d6fea2].
statements.reason: The dataset and both workloads match, but the supplied LambdaDB excerpt does not state the May 19, 2026 date.

statements.section: Performance evidence: compare workloads, not headline QPS
statements.statement: It reports Qdrant Cloud at 33.54 ms median latency, versus 78.44 ms for LambdaDB and 53.44 ms for LambdaDB with 16 partitions; Qdrant reached 391.59 QPS at 16 clients and 385.90 at 32, with 157.11 ms p95 and 0.98 Recall@10 [F-05de4589, F-198d069b, F-152aee81].
statements.reason: LambdaDB reports all the stated latency, throughput and recall figures.

statements.section: Performance evidence: compare workloads, not headline QPS
statements.statement: According to the same benchmark, Qdrant ran on three nodes, each with eight cores, 32 GB RAM, and 240 GB balanced disk, at replication factor two; that provisioned configuration cost $1,673.73 per month regardless of utilization [F-736fbde9, F-91b88665].
statements.reason: The source specifies the three-node configuration, replication factor and monthly cost regardless of utilization.

statements.section: Performance evidence: compare workloads, not headline QPS
statements.statement: Quality and query complexity change what “performance” means [F-ca893c9e, F-fb89bcc0].
statements.reason: One source evaluates retrieval relevance, while the forum report describes a complex filtered query and its latency.

statements.section: Performance evidence: compare workloads, not headline QPS
statements.statement: Weaviate reports that Search Mode improved mean Success@1 by 17% and Recall@5 by 11% over Hybrid Search across its tested benchmarks, and achieved 0.40 nDCG@10 against Hybrid Search’s 0.13 on BRIGHT Biology [F-ca893c9e, F-4081ed02].
statements.reason: Weaviate reports the average gains and the BRIGHT Biology nDCG@10 scores stated.

statements.section: Performance evidence: compare workloads, not headline QPS
statements.statement: Weaviate also reports gains over the original BRIGHT paper’s best methods of 13.4, 9.6, 2.6, 12.2, and 8.8 nDCG@10 points for Biology, Earth Science, Economics, Psychology, and Robotics, respectively; it ran three trials to account for model stochasticity and described results as fairly consistent [F-55cc424e, F-77929935].
statements.reason: The source gives all five absolute nDCG@10 gains and says it ran three fairly consistent trials.

statements.section: Performance evidence: compare workloads, not headline QPS
statements.statement: Those relevance results should not be treated as database-only QPS results [F-ca893c9e, F-77929935].
statements.reason: The cited results measure retrieval-quality metrics, not database-only queries per second.

statements.section: Performance evidence: compare workloads, not headline QPS
statements.statement: Qdrant says its filtered-ANN benchmark, published February 13, 2023, covers synthetic and real datasets with keyword through geospatial filters, and says it built a ten-billion-document benchmark with ground truth [F-53a373a8, F-2f6d7d5a, F-2b9b276d].
statements.reason: Qdrant dates the filtered-ANN post, describes the datasets and filters, and separately states it built a ten-billion-document benchmark with ground truth.

statements.section: Performance evidence: compare workloads, not headline QPS
statements.statement: At the other end of the evidence spectrum, a Weaviate forum user reported hybrid searches averaging 30 seconds and sometimes reaching two minutes over nearly 11 million objects with a cross-reference filter and vector; the user said the referenced Metadata class had nearly 50 properties and that future filter fields were not fixed [F-fb89bcc0, F-95406713].
statements.reason: The forum user reports the object count, query and filter, latency, metadata properties and uncertainty about future filter fields.

statements.section: Performance evidence: compare workloads, not headline QPS
statements.statement: That report describes one user’s query, not a comparative benchmark [F-fb89bcc0, F-95406713].
statements.reason: The forum text describes a user’s own query and does not present a comparative benchmark.

statements.section: Performance evidence: compare workloads, not headline QPS
statements.statement: According to Tech Insider, network round trips, embedding batch size, index tuning, and dataset shape can affect observed latency; Blck Alpaca reports 150–500 ms for hybrid retrieval plus cross-encoder reranking, with reranking the latency-elastic step [F-ed2cc22c, F-267cb138].
statements.reason: Tech Insider identifies the stated latency factors, and Blck Alpaca gives the reranking latency range and characterization.

statements.section: Selection guidance and a production evaluation plan
statements.statement: There is no defensible single “fastest” choice from these findings: workload shape—including filtering, scale, latency tolerance, and concurrency—can change the result [F-c490fb83].
statements.reason: The source explicitly says the fastest choice depends on filtering, scale, latency tolerance, and concurrency.

statements.section: Selection guidance and a production evaluation plan
statements.statement: The practical selection rule is to test vector databases on the team’s actual data rather than choose from vendor benchmarks [F-f1b19600].
statements.reason: The source explicitly recommends testing on actual data rather than relying on vendor benchmarks.

statements.section: Selection guidance and a production evaluation plan
statements.statement: Pinecone particularly needs a separate evaluation for direct cross-database comparison under identical conditions; an overview notes that standardized ANN-Benchmarks coverage for Weaviate and Qdrant does not provide that comparison with Pinecone [F-30e549b5].
statements.reason: The source says ANN-Benchmarks covers Weaviate and Qdrant, among others, but Pinecone requires separate evaluation, preventing a direct comparison under identical conditions.

statements.section: Selection guidance and a production evaluation plan
statements.statement: For a filter-heavy application, make selective metadata queries a prominent part of the trial rather than treating unfiltered vector recall as a sufficient proxy [F-c490fb83, F-28c23cd7].
statements.reason: The sources identify filter-heavy workloads as consequential and recommend testing combined filter-and-vector queries before choosing a database.

statements.section: Selection guidance and a production evaluation plan
statements.statement: According to medium.com, filter performance is often a greater bottleneck than improving vector recall beyond approximately 95%; that is a reason to test the claim against the application’s own queries, not an assumed threshold for every deployment [F-28c23cd7, F-f1b19600].
statements.reason: The medium.com source makes the qualified claim about recall above roughly 95% and recommends testing filter-and-vector queries; aiml.qa recommends testing on actual data.

statements.section: Selection guidance and a production evaluation plan
statements.statement: According to kalviumlabs.ai, pgvector filters the candidate set after vector search, while Qdrant applies filtering during HNSW traversal and can be materially faster for selective queries; treat this as a workload-specific claim to verify, not a settled ranking [F-71481d0c, F-c490fb83].
statements.reason: Kalviumlabs.ai explicitly describes pgvector post-filtering, Qdrant filtering during graph traversal, and faster selective queries. The workload-specific caveat is consistent with the second source.

statements.section: Selection guidance and a production evaluation plan
statements.statement: A production evaluation should use a representative query set and relevant results from the team’s data, then record Precision@K, Recall@K, and MRR for that golden set, as aiml.qa recommends [F-f1b19600, F-6fd83950].
statements.reason: Aiml.qa recommends a golden set of real queries with expected relevant documents and measuring Precision@K, Recall@K, and MRR.

statements.section: Selection guidance and a production evaluation plan
statements.statement: Run the same relevant query patterns at production-realistic QPS and measure P95 and P99 latency, including the filtering, scale, and concurrency conditions that matter to the application [F-6fd83950, F-c490fb83].
statements.reason: Aiml.qa recommends P95/P99 latency at production-realistic QPS, while the other source identifies filtering, scale, and concurrency as factors that matter.

statements.section: Selection guidance and a production evaluation plan
statements.statement: Compare candidates using both retrieval-quality and latency measurements, as aiml.qa recommends [F-6fd83950].
statements.reason: Aiml.qa recommends measuring both retrieval quality and query latency for candidate databases.

statements.section: Selection guidance and a production evaluation plan
statements.statement: As one limited planning reference, ranksquire.com estimated roughly $30–60 per month, varying by region, for a Qdrant Cloud Standard cluster with 2GB RAM, 1 vCPU, and 20GB disk; the team’s test must establish whether that configuration meets its own quality and latency requirements [F-1b54c829, F-6fd83950].
statements.reason: Ranksquire.com gives that configuration and regional monthly estimate as directional; aiml.qa recommends testing candidates against the team's own data for quality and latency.
